p01-compare-title.name: p01-compare-title
p01-compare-title.text: Of two boundaries that both separate the data, which is "safer"?

p01-compare-ctx.name: p01-compare-ctx
p01-compare-ctx.text: Four points: positive (circles) $(1,1),(1,-1)$; negative (triangles) $(-1,1),(-1,-1)$. Both line A and line B separate them.

p01-compare-src.name: p01-compare-src
p01-compare-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture §1 (the boundary is not unique); comparing by "how far the nearest point is from the line" is a teaching choice, and the next page writes it as a formula in $\mathbf w,b$.

p01-compare-c0.name: p01-compare-c0
p01-compare-c0.text: How do we measure "safe"? First fix a measure: look at how far the nearest point is from the line, the farther the better.

p01-compare-lA.name: p01-compare-lA
p01-compare-lA.text: Line A (green): the nearest point is $1$ from the line

p01-compare-lB.name: p01-compare-lB
p01-compare-lB.text: Line B (orange): the nearest point is $\dfrac{|2\cdot1+1\cdot(-1)|}{\sqrt{2^2+1^2}}=0.447$ from the line

p01-compare-c3.name: p01-compare-c3
p01-compare-c3.text: A's nearest point is farther, so A is safer. Next: write this distance as a formula in $\mathbf w,b$.

p02-normalize-title.name: p02-normalize-title
p02-normalize-title.text: If we scale the score, does the boundary move? What are the half-width γ and the full width W?

p02-normalize-ctx.name: p02-normalize-ctx
p02-normalize-ctx.text: Score $g=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b$. The distance from a point to the line is $|g|/\|\mathbf w\|$; now check what happens when $(\mathbf w,b)$ are all multiplied by $k$.

p02-normalize-src.name: p02-normalize-src
p02-normalize-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture §1 (scaling does not move the boundary); $k=0.5,1,2$ is a teaching example; the lecture's "margin 1" means the half-width $\gamma$ and its "full width 2" means $W$.

p02-normalize-c0.name: p02-normalize-c0
p02-normalize-c0.text: The point $(1,1)$ is 1 unit above the decision line $x_1=0$, distance $=1$.

p02-normalize-c2.name: p02-normalize-c2
p02-normalize-c2.text: Choose $k$ so the nearest point's score is exactly $1$ (normalization): $y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)\ge1$. The purple dashed lines are $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b=\pm1$.

p02-normalize-c3.name: p02-normalize-c3
p02-normalize-c3.text: Half-width $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\|\mathbf w\|}=1$: decision line to supporting line

p02-normalize-c4.name: p02-normalize-c4
p02-normalize-c4.text: Full width $W=\dfrac{2}{\|\mathbf w\|}=2$ (between the two supporting lines). $\gamma$ and $W$ differ by a factor of two; do not mix them.

p03-feasible-title.name: p03-feasible-title
p03-feasible-title.text: "Maximum margin" written as a minimization: which w are allowed, which one is smallest?

p03-feasible-ctx.name: p03-feasible-ctx
p03-feasible-ctx.text: Maximizing $\gamma=1/\|\mathbf w\|$ equals minimizing $\|\mathbf w\|$. This page fixes $b=0$ (a teaching setting: the data are symmetric; the full problem's numerical solution also has $b=0$).

p03-feasible-src.name: p03-feasible-src
p03-feasible-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture §2 rewritten as a minimum weight norm; the $\mathbf w$-plane plot is added by this task, and a QP numerical check gives $\mathbf w=(1,0)$, $b=0$.

p03-feasible-c0.name: p03-feasible-c0
p03-feasible-c0.text: $\min_{\mathbf w}\ \tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2\quad\text{s.t.}\ y_i\,\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i\ge1$. Each $(w_1,w_2)$ in the plot is a candidate boundary.

p03-feasible-c1.name: p03-feasible-c1
p03-feasible-c1.text: Each point gives one constraint: points 1 and 4 give $w_1+w_2\ge1$ (blue line), points 2 and 3 give $w_1-w_2\ge1$ (purple line). Four points produce only two distinct lines; the green region is where both hold.

p03-feasible-c2.name: p03-feasible-c2
p03-feasible-c2.text: The contours of the objective $\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2$ are circles centered at the origin: the smaller the radius the better (radii $0.5,1,1.5$).

p03-feasible-c3.name: p03-feasible-c3
p03-feasible-c3.text: The smallest circle in the feasible region just touches the vertex $(1,0)$: optimum $\mathbf w^{\ast}=(1,0)$, $\|\mathbf w^{\ast}\|=1$, $W=2/\|\mathbf w^{\ast}\|=2$.

p04-multiplier-title.name: p04-multiplier-title
p04-multiplier-title.text: Is a constraint "pushing"? First see the multiplier α in one dimension

p04-multiplier-ctx.name: p04-multiplier-ctx
p04-multiplier-ctx.text: One dimension: minimize $f(w)=\tfrac12w^2$, but $w$ must satisfy a constraint. The constraint is like a wall: it pushes you only when you touch it.

p04-multiplier-src.name: p04-multiplier-src
p04-multiplier-src.text: Source: The one-dimensional multiplier example is added by this task (audience: optimization is new); it corresponds to the Lagrange multiplier and complementary slackness of lecture §3.

p04-multiplier-fgL.name: p04-multiplier-fgL
p04-multiplier-fgL.text: The objective slopes down to the lower left: slope $w^{\ast}=1$

p04-multiplier-c1.name: p04-multiplier-c1
p04-multiplier-c1.text: Balance: $w^{\ast}=\alpha\cdot1$, so $\alpha=1$. A wall can only push, not pull: $\alpha\ge0$.

p04-multiplier-fgR.name: p04-multiplier-fgR
p04-multiplier-fgR.text: Slope $0$ at the valley: no wall needed

p04-multiplier-c2.name: p04-multiplier-c2
p04-multiplier-c2.text: The wall is not touched: $\alpha=0$. Only a touching constraint can push ($\alpha>0$).

p04-multiplier-c3.name: p04-multiplier-c3
p04-multiplier-c3.text: Multiplier $\alpha$ = the force the constraint exerts: $\alpha\ge0$; $\alpha=0$ when not touching.

p05-force-balance-title.name: p05-force-balance-title
p05-force-balance-title.text: Back to the SVM: both constraints are touching; how much force does each exert to hold up w*?

p05-force-balance-ctx.name: p05-force-balance-ctx
p05-force-balance-ctx.text: The same $\mathbf w$ plane. At the optimum $(1,0)$ both the blue and purple lines are touching, and the objective's "slope" is $\mathbf w^{\ast}=(1,0)$.

p05-force-balance-src.name: p05-force-balance-src
p05-force-balance-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture §3 dual and complementary slackness ($\mathbf w=\sum\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i$); the force-balance picture and the choice $\alpha=\tfrac14$ are teaching additions, with numbers checked.

p05-force-balance-c0.name: p05-force-balance-c0
p05-force-balance-c0.text: The "wall" of constraint $i$ pushes toward $y_i\mathbf x_i$ (negatives are multiplied by $-1$): point 1: $(1,1)$; point 4: $(-1)\cdot(-1,-1)=(1,1)$ (blue circles); point 2: $(1,-1)$; point 3: $(-1)\cdot(-1,1)=(1,-1)$ (purple circles).

p05-force-balance-c1.name: p05-force-balance-c1
p05-force-balance-c1.text: The blue-line group (the blue circles in the data plane, points 1 and 4) together exert force $\tfrac12$: $\tfrac12\times(1,1)$.

p05-force-balance-c2.name: p05-force-balance-c2
p05-force-balance-c2.text: The purple-line group (purple circles, points 2 and 3) also exerts $\tfrac12$: attached after it, $\tfrac12\times(1,-1)$.

p05-force-balance-c3.name: p05-force-balance-c3
p05-force-balance-c3.text: The two forces add to $(1,0)=\mathbf w^{\ast}$: holding up the optimum. $\mathbf w^{\ast}=\tfrac12(1,1)+\tfrac12(1,-1)$.

p05-force-balance-c4.name: p05-force-balance-c4
p05-force-balance-c4.text: Back to the data points: $\mathbf w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i$; in this example all four points touch, take $\alpha_i=\tfrac14$ ($\sum\alpha_iy_i=0$). Prediction depends only on points with $\alpha_i>0$.

p06-move-title.name: p06-move-title
p06-move-title.text: If we move one point, does the optimal boundary change?

p06-move-ctx.name: p06-move-ctx
p06-move-ctx.text: Back to the data plane. The original solution: $\mathbf w=(1,0)$, $b=0$ (green line), supporting lines $x_1=\pm1$. Add a positive point $\mathbf x_5$ and see where placing it changes the solution.

p06-move-src.name: p06-move-src
p06-move-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture §5 influence of unrelated points; the three positions of $\mathbf x_5$ are teaching choices, and the new solutions are obtained by QP (compute_data.kp14x).

p06-move-c0.name: p06-move-c0
p06-move-c0.text: Full width $W$ = the distance between the two supporting lines = $2/\|\mathbf w\|$ (original $W=2$, the purple double arrow above). A point outside the band does not touch its constraint, $\alpha=0$.

p06-move-c1.name: p06-move-c1
p06-move-c1.text: $\mathbf x_5=(3,0.5)$: score $=3\ge1$, outside the band, not touching $\Rightarrow\alpha_5=0$. Removing it leaves the solution unchanged: $\mathbf w=(1,0)$, $W=2$.

p06-move-c2.name: p06-move-c2
p06-move-c2.text: Moved to $(1.5,0.5)$: score $=1.5$, still outside the band, solution unchanged ($\mathbf w=(1,0)$, $W=2$).

p06-move-c3.name: p06-move-c3
p06-move-c3.text: Moved to $(0.6,0.5)$: its score is only $0.6<1$, so the original solution no longer satisfies the constraint and we must re-solve: $\mathbf w=(1.25,0)$, $b=0.25$. The new point and $(-1,\pm1)$ touch, replaced by the orange boundary; the orange double arrow (below, from $x_1=-1$ to $0.6$) is the new full width $W=2/1.25=1.6$, narrower than the original $2$.

p06-move-c4.name: p06-move-c4
p06-move-c4.text: Only points that touch or cross the line decide the solution; moving a point outside the band without crossing leaves the solution unchanged.

p07-nonunique-title.name: p07-nonunique-title
p07-nonunique-title.text: [Optional] The boundary is unique, so why is there a whole family of multipliers?

p07-nonunique-ctx.name: p07-nonunique-ctx
p07-nonunique-ctx.text: Points 1 and 4 share a normal vector, as do points 2 and 3: the force fixes only the sum per group, and any split within a group holds it up.

p07-nonunique-src.name: p07-nonunique-src
p07-nonunique-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture §4 square example's multiplier family $(t,\tfrac12-t,t,\tfrac12-t)$; the "repeated normal vectors" explanation is a teaching addition; marked optional.

p07-nonunique-c0.name: p07-nonunique-c0
p07-nonunique-c0.text: The sum of each group's forces is fixed: $\alpha_1+\alpha_4=\tfrac12$, $\alpha_2+\alpha_3=\tfrac12$. However it is split within a group, $\mathbf w$ is $(1,0)$.

p07-nonunique-c4.name: p07-nonunique-c4
p07-nonunique-c4.text: Three different multiplier sets, the same $\mathbf w^{\ast}=(1,0)$: the boundary is unique, the multipliers are not.

p08-practice-title.name: p08-practice-title
p08-practice-title.text: Practice: positives 3, 4, 5, negatives $−1$, $−2$: find the decision point, full width and touching points

p08-practice-ctx.name: p08-practice-ctx
p08-practice-ctx.text: Work it out first. Hint: first find the closest pair of the two classes, the decision point is between them; touching points have scores of exactly $\pm1$. Press Next when done.

p08-practice-src.name: p08-practice-src
p08-practice-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture practice; answer computed by compute_data.kp14()["prac"].

p08-practice-q.name: p08-practice-q
p08-practice-q.text: (a) The decision point $x^{\ast}$?  (b) The full margin width $W$?  (c) Which points touch the supporting lines (multipliers may be positive)?

p08-practice-a1.name: p08-practice-a1
p08-practice-a1.text: (a) The closest pair is $3$ and $-1$: decision point $x^{\ast}=1$

p08-practice-a3.name: p08-practice-a3
p08-practice-a3.text: (c) The touching points are $3$ and $-1$ ($\alpha>0$); $4,5,-2$ are outside the band ($\alpha=0$)

p09-summary-title.name: p09-summary-title
p09-summary-title.text: Summary: from "safe distance" to support vectors

p09-summary-ctx.name: p09-summary-ctx
p09-summary-ctx.text: Recall along the same $\mathbf w$ plane: the feasible region, the optimum and the two groups of forces; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p09-summary-e0.name: p09-summary-e0
p09-summary-e0.text: Compare boundaries by "the nearest point's distance": $\gamma=1/\|\mathbf w\|$, $W=2/\|\mathbf w\|$; scaling $(\mathbf w,b)$ does not change the boundary

p09-summary-e1.name: p09-summary-e1
p09-summary-e1.text: Maximum margin $\Leftrightarrow$ $\min\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2$ s.t. $y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)\ge1$; in the $\mathbf w$ plane find the smallest circle in the feasible region

p09-summary-e2.name: p09-summary-e2
p09-summary-e2.text: Multiplier $\alpha$ = the force the constraint exerts, $\alpha\ge0$; only touching constraints can push, $\alpha=0$ when not touching

p09-summary-e3.name: p09-summary-e3
p09-summary-e3.text: $\mathbf w=\sum\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i$: only support vectors take part; moving a point outside the band without crossing leaves the solution unchanged

p09-summary-e4.name: p09-summary-e4
p09-summary-e4.text: Optional: multipliers may be non-unique. Next KP: relax the constraints when data are not separable (soft margin)

frame-u01.name: frame-u01

p04-multiplier-cdef.name: p04-multiplier-cdef
p04-multiplier-cdef.text: Multiplier $\alpha$: give each constraint a push coefficient. No contact, no push ($\alpha=0$); contact pushes ($\alpha>0$); it pushes but never pulls ($\alpha\ge0$).

p10-lagrangian-title.text: The Lagrangian and two zero partial derivatives: why $\mathbf w$ is a weighted sum of data points
p10-lagrangian-title.name: p10-lagrangian-title

p10-lagrangian-ctx.text: Primal $\min\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2$ subject to $y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)\ge1$: put a multiplier $\alpha_i\ge0$ (the push coefficient of the last page) on each constraint to fold the constraints into the objective.
p10-lagrangian-ctx.name: p10-lagrangian-ctx

p10-lagrangian-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture §2 "going further" (the Lagrangian and its partial derivatives); the example reuses the four square points with $\alpha=\tfrac14$, recomputed independently. Added page: the full dual restored from the lecture objectives.
p10-lagrangian-src.name: p10-lagrangian-src

p10-lagrangian-c0.text: $L(\mathbf w,b,\boldsymbol\alpha)=\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2+\sum_i\alpha_i\left[1-y_i(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i+b)\right],\quad\alpha_i\ge0$. A violated constraint adds a penalty; only constraints on the edge can have $\alpha_i>0$.
p10-lagrangian-c0.name: p10-lagrangian-c0

p10-lagrangian-c1.text: Take the partial derivative in $\mathbf w$ and set it to $0$: $\nabla_{\mathbf w}L=\mathbf w-\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i=0\ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i$.
p10-lagrangian-c1.name: p10-lagrangian-c1

p10-lagrangian-c2.text: Take the partial derivative in $b$ and set it to $0$: $\partial L/\partial b=-\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0\ \Rightarrow\ \sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0$.
p10-lagrangian-c2.name: p10-lagrangian-c2

p10-lagrangian-c3.text: Square example (with $\alpha_i=\tfrac14$): $y_i\mathbf x_i=(1,1),(1,-1),(1,-1),(1,1)$. The four pieces $\tfrac14y_i\mathbf x_i$ chain head to tail and end at $\mathbf w=(1,0)$.
p10-lagrangian-c3.name: p10-lagrangian-c3

p10-lagrangian-c5.text: Meaning: $\mathbf w$ is a weighted sum of data points and only points with $\alpha_i>0$ appear; $\sum\alpha_iy_i=0$ requires the forces of the positive and negative classes to be equal. The next page uses a two-dimensional example to see how hard each constraint pushes; the one after substitutes back to get the dual problem in $\boldsymbol\alpha$ only.
p10-lagrangian-c5.name: p10-lagrangian-c5

p10-lagrangian-cue1.text: See the blue card: the partial derivative in $\mathbf w$.
p10-lagrangian-cue1.name: p10-lagrangian-cue1

p10-lagrangian-cue2.text: See the green card: the partial derivative in $b$.
p10-lagrangian-cue2.name: p10-lagrangian-cue2

p10-lagrangian-cue3.text: See the plot: four vectors chain head to tail to $\mathbf w=(1,0)$.

p11-dual-title.text: Substitute and eliminate: the dual problem, complementary slackness and the prediction formula
p11-dual-title.name: p11-dual-title

p11-dual-ctx.text: Following the force balance: substitute $\mathbf w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i$ and $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0$ into $L$ to leave only $\boldsymbol\alpha$; verify with the square example that the dual value equals the primal value.
p11-dual-ctx.name: p11-dual-ctx

p11-dual-src.text: Source: KP14 lecture §3 (dual and complementary slackness) and §4 (square example); $G$ and the dual value recomputed independently. Added page: the full dual restored from the lecture objectives.
p11-dual-src.name: p11-dual-src

p11-dual-c0.text: Substituting: $\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x_j$; $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_i$ is the same sum; $b\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0$.
p11-dual-c0.name: p11-dual-c0

p11-dual-c1.text: Collecting terms gives $L=\sum_i\alpha_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x_j$, and the dual problem is $\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\left[\sum_i\alpha_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x_j\right],\ \alpha_i\ge0,\ \sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0$.
p11-dual-c1.name: p11-dual-c1

p11-dual-c2.text: Square example: for $\boldsymbol\alpha=\tfrac14(1,1,1,1)^T$, $\boldsymbol\alpha^TG\boldsymbol\alpha=\tfrac{16}{16}=1$ and the dual value is $\sum\alpha_i-\tfrac12(1)=1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$.
p11-dual-c2.name: p11-dual-c2

p11-dual-c3.text: The primal value is $\tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2=\tfrac12$: both sides are equal (zero duality gap), so $\boldsymbol\alpha=\tfrac14\mathbf 1$ is one optimal multiplier (the problem is convex).
p11-dual-c3.name: p11-dual-c3

p11-dual-c4.text: Complementary slackness: $\alpha_i\left[y_ig_i-1\right]=0$. A point with $\alpha_i>0$ must lie on a support plane (the converse need not hold; degenerate data are exceptions). Here all four points have $y_ig_i=1$ and sit on the edge.
p11-dual-c4.name: p11-dual-c4

p11-dual-c5.text: Prediction uses only inner products: $g(\mathbf x)=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf x_i^T\mathbf x+b$, here $g(\mathbf x)=x_1$. The inner-product form is the entrance to kernel methods, but computing inner products still depends on the feature dimension.
p11-dual-c5.name: p11-dual-c5
